body:
North India after the Guptas

By the late 6th century CE, the decline of Gupta power had left northern India divided among regional kingdoms. One was ruled by the Pushyabhuti or Vardhana dynasty, based at Sthaneshvara (Thanesar, in present-day Haryana). Another was the Maukhari kingdom of Kanyakubja (Kannauj, in present-day Uttar Pradesh). The rulers of Gauda in Bengal were an important eastern power.

Harshavardhana (Harsha) belonged to the Vardhana family. His reign is generally dated 606–647 CE. He began as ruler of Thanesar and subsequently made Kannauj his principal centre of power. These were different cities, not alternative names for the same capital.

The family crisis that brought Harsha to power

PersonConnection with HarshaPolitical role
PrabhakaravardhanaFatherRuler of Thanesar
RajyavardhanaElder brotherSucceeded their father at Thanesar
RajyashriSisterMarried into the Maukhari family of Kannauj
GrahavarmanBrother-in-lawMaukhari ruler of Kannauj

After Prabhakaravardhana died, Rajyavardhana became ruler of Thanesar. A conflict then broke out around Kannauj: Devagupta of Malwa attacked the Maukharis, Grahavarman was killed, and Rajyashri was taken prisoner. Rajyavardhana defeated the Malwa forces but was subsequently killed. The account associated with Harsha's court attributes his death to Shashanka, ruler of Gauda (Bengal).

Harsha succeeded his elder brother at Thanesar in 606 CE. He rescued Rajyashri and took control of Kannauj, linking the Vardhana and Maukhari political centres. Kannauj, located in the fertile and well-connected Ganga plain, became his main seat of government.

Thanesar was the Vardhana family's earlier seat; Kannauj was the Maukhari centre that became Harsha's principal capital. His rule began in 606 CE, but it did not begin with the conquest of the whole subcontinent.

Prelims focus

  • Dynasty: Pushyabhuti, also called Vardhana.
  • Reign: 606–647 CE; initial seat: Thanesar.
  • Later capital: Kannauj or Kanyakubja.
  • Rajyashri was married to Grahavarman of the Maukhari dynasty.
  • Shashanka ruled Gauda; Devagupta was associated with Malwa.
  • Trap: The Maukharis ruled Kannauj before Harsha established his principal seat there.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, ch. 11, pp. 114–115 (2018–19 edition); IGNOU, History of India from c. 300 C.E. to 1206, BHIC-132, Unit 3, pp. 35–39 (2019).]

title: Harsha’s rise: from Thanesar to Kannauj

body:
Expansion in the north and east

Once he held Thanesar and Kannauj, Harsha sought to strengthen his authority in the Ganga valley and beyond. His chief eastern rival was Shashanka of Gauda, based in Bengal. Harsha formed an alliance with Bhaskaravarman, ruler of Kamarupa (in the Assam region), which put pressure on Shashanka from another direction.

Harsha's campaigns and influence subsequently reached Magadha and parts of Bengal and Odisha. His power was not identical everywhere: some places were governed more directly, while other rulers retained their own kingdoms and acknowledged his superiority or remained allies. Shashanka's continued power for much of his lifetime is an important reason not to treat Harsha's early eastern campaigns as an immediate conquest of all Bengal.

The Narmada and the Chalukya check

Harsha attempted to expand southward towards the Deccan, but his advance was checked near the Narmada River by Pulakeshin II, the ruler of the Chalukyas of Badami. Pulakeshin's court poet Ravikirti celebrated this success in the Aihole inscription.

The result is commonly described as Harsha's defeat or failure to cross into the Deccan. The essential geographical distinction is that Harsha was a dominant power in northern India, not the ruler of the Chalukya Deccan. The Chalukyas and the Pallavas were different southern dynasties; it was Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas who checked Harsha.

Gujarat: Vallabhi and the Maitrakas

Vallabhi (Valabhi) in Saurashtra, Gujarat, was the capital of the Maitraka dynasty. Harsha's relations with the Maitrakas included conflict and later political accommodation. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang's account indicates that Dhruvasena II of Vallabhi became Harsha's son-in-law; the marriage is understood as a political alliance.

This is a genuine Gujarat connection, but it does not mean that every part of Gujarat became an ordinary province of Harsha's empire. Vallabhi remained a regional political centre under its Maitraka rulers.

Direct rule, subordinate allegiance and alliance are different relationships. A king who sent tribute or joined a royal assembly did not necessarily surrender day-to-day control of his territory.

Prelims focus

  • Shashanka: ruler of Gauda and Harsha's eastern rival.
  • Bhaskaravarman: ruler of Kamarupa and Harsha's ally.
  • Pulakeshin II: Chalukya ruler who checked Harsha near the Narmada.
  • Ravikirti: composer of Pulakeshin II's Aihole inscription.
  • Dhruvasena II: Maitraka ruler of Vallabhi, linked to Harsha by marriage.
  • Trap: The Narmada campaign did not bring the Chalukya Deccan under Harsha's rule.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, ch. 11, pp. 115–116 (2018–19 edition); IGNOU, History of India from c. 300 C.E. to 1206, BHIC-132, Unit 3, pp. 39–41 (2019); Annette Schmiedchen, “Maitrakas,” The Encyclopedia of Ancient History (2021), section on Harsha and Dhruvasena II, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Harsha’s campaigns, rivals and the Gujarat connection

body:
The king and his officers

Harsha was the central figure in government. He directed military campaigns, appointed leading officials and received advice from ministers. Titles such as Maharajadhiraja (“great king over kings”) expressed sovereign rank; they did not mean that every king in India was directly administered from Kannauj.

Xuanzang portrayed Harsha as an active ruler who travelled through his territories, supervised affairs and met people. These tours mattered because orders issued at the centre had to be carried out by regional officers, local chiefs and village authorities across a large area.

From province to village

Harsha's government retained important features of the preceding Gupta administrative pattern. A bhukti was a province, a vishaya a district and a grama a village. A village was the basic local unit and an important source of agricultural revenue. The terms express levels of administration; they do not show that every region had exactly the same officials or degree of central control.

Land revenue, soldiers and local chiefs

Agriculture provided the main regular source of revenue. Xuanzang describes a royal share of roughly one-sixth of agricultural produce; this is an account of the levy, not proof that every cultivator in every locality paid an identical amount. Rulers also received tribute from subordinate chiefs. Some officials or military supporters were rewarded with rights over land or its revenue instead of only cash salaries.

The army included infantry, cavalry and war elephants. In addition to troops maintained by the ruler, samantas—subordinate chiefs or important landed military supporters—could be required to supply soldiers. Their relationship with the king depended on his strength: a loyal samanta helped royal campaigns, while a powerful one might seek greater independence.

A large moving army and court also affected ordinary villagers. Banabhatta describes local people providing food and fodder to a royal entourage and sometimes bringing petitions to the king; he also describes the damage that soldiers and animals could cause. Political authority therefore involved both royal commands and practical demands on local communities.

Prelims focus

  • Administrative terms: bhukti = province; vishaya = district; grama = village.
  • Agricultural produce was the leading source of regular state revenue.
  • Xuanzang reported a royal land-revenue share of about one-sixth.
  • Samantas provided military support and might receive land-revenue rights.
  • Harsha's army included infantry, cavalry and elephants.
  • Trap: A samanta was a subordinate chief, not automatically a salaried official of the central government.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, ch. 11, pp. 116–119 (2018–19 edition); IGNOU, History of India from c. 300 C.E. to 1206, BHIC-132, Unit 3, pp. 41–42 (2019); P. Bhaskar Reddy, “Harshavardhana,” Outlines of Indian History, INFLIBNET, §§6–7, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Harsha’s administration: royal power, revenue and samantas

body:
Who was Xuanzang?

Xuanzang (also written Xuan Zang or Hiuen Tsang) was a Chinese Buddhist monk and pilgrim who visited India during Harsha's reign, commonly dated to about 630–643 CE. He travelled to places associated with the Buddha, visited monasteries, studied Buddhist learning and spent time at Harsha's court.

Xuanzang studied at Nalanda, the major Buddhist monastic centre of learning in present-day Bihar. Its scholars taught religious philosophy and maintained a rigorous intellectual life. Xuanzang collected Sanskrit Buddhist works and took more than 600 manuscripts back towards China, where he devoted much of his later life to translation.

What Xuanzang observed

His travel record, generally called the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (also known as Si-yu-ki), describes places, monasteries, religious practices and political conditions. He portrayed Harsha as an energetic ruler with a large army, a keen interest in religious discussion and a practice of charitable giving. Xuanzang also attended Harsha's celebrated assemblies at Kannauj and Prayag.

Distinguishing the main names and works

PersonWork or recordConnection to Harsha
Banabhatta (Bana)HarshacharitaSanskrit court biography that narrates Harsha's rise to kingship
XuanzangGreat Tang Records on the Western RegionsChinese pilgrim's description of places and conditions during Harsha's reign
RavikirtiAihole inscriptionChalukya court account celebrating Pulakeshin II's check of Harsha

These accounts describe different things. The Harshacharita focuses on the ruler's family and accession; it does not narrate the entire 606–647 CE reign. Xuanzang supplies observations from his travels, while the Aihole inscription presents a rival ruler's military success. They are useful together, but a royal eulogy should not be read as an exact description of every political boundary.

Do not confuse the Chinese pilgrims: Fa Xian visited India earlier, during the Gupta period; Xuanzang visited during Harsha's reign; and I-Qing (Yijing) came later.

Prelims focus

  • Xuanzang: Chinese Buddhist pilgrim during Harsha's reign.
  • Nalanda: major Buddhist learning centre in present-day Bihar.
  • Xuanzang returned with more than 600 Buddhist manuscripts.
  • Banabhatta wrote Harshacharita in Sanskrit.
  • Ravikirti wrote the Aihole inscription about Pulakeshin II.
  • Trap: The Harshacharita was written by Bana, not by Harsha.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, ch. 10, pp. 105–106, and ch. 11, p. 114 (2018–19 edition); NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, ch. 2 “Kings, Farmers and Towns,” p. 40; IGNOU, History of India from c. 300 C.E. to 1206, BHIC-132, Unit 3, §§3.4.1 and 3.4.4 (2019).]
